chapter: Theater work, first jobs and recording credits
title: Starting jobs, being called a ham, and passing other trombonists
summary: He was working within months, was called a ham, studied hard and out-played the trombonists his age.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: But how old were you about when you started playing jobs in around Chicago?

Oh I started playing about, I was playing pretty good in eight months. You were about 19 or something like that? I always did get a fair tone you know. It was a Mexican show, just a solid tone. Yeah. And so then I, then they formed a band. There's two Simeon brothers which is from New Orleans. Yeah. And there was Jimmy Mackenzie on the drum, myself and Bernie and sometimes Dominic. And so Richard Jones on piano, one time he had the band.
So you started working pretty fast after you.
Yeah I didn't let no grass grow my feet. No. No I started. But did you become a professional musician?
Huh? You started becoming a professional musician.

Yeah well the guys would call me Ham. You see when they think you didn't play so well they call you Ham. Yeah right. And so I was determined to make some of those guys eat the woods which I did. When I went up in, when I traveled in Wisconsin and Michigan and Minnesota, I studied hard. And then I got another teacher in Milwaukee as I foreseed. And so I was surprised with a fellow drum motor named Harry Swift, he was Charles Ellick's band, the Wisconsin Roof. That's before Simeon had it. I was still with Eli Wright. And so he stood behind me one night. And so I knew he was behind me so I did my best. So he said boy how did you play that? So I began to think, I said well this is supposed to be one of the number one aces and here he is asking me how did I play it. So I said I played it like this. He said well I've been trying to play it ever since. So when I did, after I left the Wisconsin Roof and Bernie Young, around there, these same guys let the time catch it with them see. There was a bunch of us in the same category around there, good trombone players like, let's see, myself, it was about five of us around the same age. Well we were studying and these other guys, Billy Franklin was one of myself, he played with Jeffrey Tavern, he played at Wisconsin Roof, I've taken his place up there. He left there to go to Huey Swift at Jeffrey Tavern, he wanted to come back home see. We had Mondays off but he wanted to be around his wife. So those guys, I used to notice them, they'd sit around at the poker table, at the poker table in time to go to work. Then he'd come right back and play the rest of the night and all day. And they did that for years. And I'm studying. So after a while I caught up with them and I passed them. Well then they began to get serious you know. They wasn't calling me to harm so much then because they found out that I had surpassed them, not only me, but all the young trombone players around there, John Thomas and a bunch of us. Al Wynn, he's from yours here, he died recently. And so then it tickled me, I said uh-huh, I got you now. And I just made them study more. Then when I went going to Regal, that opened the eyes because I had got this education, you understand. And I know what I was doing. The thing is, you know what you're doing. If you make one nice note, it's better than three bedrooms. See I'm teaching in Chicago now.
